title: Additivity of abstract Tate residues in an exact sequence
statement:
Let $k$ be a field and $R$ a commutative $k$-algebra. Let $0\to V_1\xrightarrow{i}V\xrightarrow{q}V_3\to0$ be an exact sequence of $R$-modules: $i$ is injective, $q$ is surjective and $\operatorname{im}i=\ker q$. Let $A\subset V$ be an admissible $k$-linear subspace, in the sense and with the residue maps $\operatorname{res}_{V,A}:\Omega^1_{R/k}\to k$ of [lem-pc-tate-abstract-residue-calculus]. Then $i^{-1}(A)\subset V_1$ and $q(A)\subset V_3$ are admissible, and the following identity holds as maps $\Omega^1_{R/k}\to k$:
$$\operatorname{res}_{V,A}=\operatorname{res}_{V_1,i^{-1}A}+\operatorname{res}_{V_3,q(A)}.$$

source.place: §1 property (T2) and §2 Theorem 1: exact-sequence consequence with a projection preserving im(i). Project declaration TateResidue.res_eq_add_of_exact, WeilConjectures/RingTheory/TateResidue/ResidueProperties.lean:55–116.

proof.text: Put $N=i(V_1)=\ker q$, $I=A\cap N$, and let $p:V\to V/N$ be the quotient map. The admissibility definition in [lem-pc-tate-abstract-residue-calculus] applies to $I\subset N$: for each $r\in R$, the inclusion induces an injection $(rI+I)/I\hookrightarrow(rA+A)/A$, since $rI+I\subset N$ and $A\cap N=I$. Its target is finite-dimensional. Likewise $(r p(A)+p(A))/p(A)$ is a quotient of $(rA+A)/A$, by the map induced by $p$, and is finite-dimensional. Thus $I\subset N$ and $p(A)\subset V/N$ are admissible. The maps $i:V_1\to N$ and $\bar q:V/N\to V_3$, $v+N\mapsto q(v)$, are $R$-linear isomorphisms: injectivity uses respectively the given injectivity of $i$ and $\ker q=N$, and surjectivity uses the definitions of $N$ and the surjectivity of $q$. They carry $i^{-1}(A)$ to $I$ and $p(A)$ to $q(A)$. The same quotient spaces under these isomorphisms prove both admissibility clauses in the item.

source.place: §2, admissibility condition preceding Theorem 1; elementary subspace and quotient argument

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-vector-subspace-complement] to choose $k$-linear complements $A=I\oplus B$, $N=I\oplus C$, and $V=(A+N)\oplus D$. Then $A+N=I\oplus B\oplus C$: if $u+b+c=0$ with $u\in I$, $b\in B$, $c\in C$, then $b=-(u+c)\in A\cap N=I$, hence $b=0$, and then $u=c=0$. Define the $k$-linear projection $\pi$ on $V=I\oplus B\oplus C\oplus D$ by $\pi(u+b+c+d)=u+b$. It has image $A$, fixes $A$, and preserves $N$. Its restriction $\pi_N$ is a projection of $N$ onto $I$. The formula $\bar\pi(v+N)=\pi(v)+N$ is well-defined, has image $p(A)$, and fixes $p(A)$, so is a projection on $V/N$. No $R$-linear splitting of the exact sequence is used.

source.place: §1 (T2), p. 150, and §2 Theorem 1, pp. 151–152; compatible projections constructed by vector-space complements

proof.text: Fix $f,g\in R$ and write $m_f,m_g$ for their multiplication operators. By [lem-pc-tate-abstract-residue-calculus], $T=[\pi m_f,m_g]$ is finite-potent and $\operatorname{res}_{V,A}(f\,dg)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{fp},V}(T)$. Because $N$ is an $R$-submodule and $\pi(N)\subset N$, $T(N)\subset N$. Restricting the expression $\pi(fgv)-g\pi(fv)$ to $N$ gives $T|_N=[\pi_N m_f,m_g]$, with multiplication now on $N$. Applying $p$ to that expression gives $\overline T=[\bar\pi m_f,m_g]$ on $V/N$. The same cited residue formula, using the admissibility proved in step 1 and the projections in step 2, identifies their finite-potent traces with $\operatorname{res}_{N,I}(f\,dg)$ and $\operatorname{res}_{V/N,p(A)}(f\,dg)$.

source.place: §2 Theorem 1 and Remark, pp. 151–152, commutator formula for a projection

proof.text: Apply the stable-subspace additivity clause of [lem-pc-finite-potent-trace-calculus] to the finite-potent $T$ and its stable subspace $N$. It yields $\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{fp},V}(T)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{fp},N}(T|_N)+\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{fp},V/N}(\overline T)$. Substituting step 3 proves the desired residue equality on $f\,dg$ for the pairs $(N,I)$ and $(V/N,p(A))$. Invariance under $R$-linear isomorphisms of pairs in [lem-pc-tate-abstract-residue-calculus], applied to the two explicit isomorphisms of step 1, replaces these residues by $\operatorname{res}_{V_1,i^{-1}(A)}$ and $\operatorname{res}_{V_3,q(A)}$.

source.place: §1 property (T2), p. 150; §2 Theorem 1 and invariance of the residue, pp. 151–152

proof.text: All three residue maps are $k$-linear by [lem-pc-tate-abstract-residue-calculus]. By the generators-and-relations description in [def-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials], every differential is a finite sum $\sum_j f_j\,dg_j$: an $R$-linear combination of the generators $dg$ has exactly this form. Applying the equality of step 4 to every term and adding proves equality of the maps on $\Omega^1_{R/k}$.

source.place: §2 Theorem 1, pp. 151–152, surjectivity of the map sending f tensor g to f dg

reviewed.note: mechanical checks by tools/merge_delivery.py; mathematics reviewed in full by NT-cc-Q79-2ff05be00 (reviewer sub-agent of L); spot-checked: Statement is byte-identical to the base (base: unsplit, empty proof). No new nodes and no repair note. Step 1: I=A∩N is admissible because (rI+I)/I injects into (rA+A)/A, using rI+I⊂N and A∩N=I. p(A) is admissible because its quotient space is a quotient of (rA+A)/A. i:V1→N and q̄:V/N→V3 are R-isomorphisms carrying i⁻¹A to I and p(A) to q(A). Step 2: I⊕B⊕C is direct (b∈A∩N=I∩B=0). π(u+b+c+d)=u+b fixes A and sends N to I, so π_N and π̄ are well-defined projections. Step 3: T=[πm_f,m_g] preserves N, with T|_N=[π_N m_f,m_g] and the induced map on V/N equal to [π̄ m_f,m_g]. This sign matches Tate Thm 1 and abstract-residue-calculus. Step 4: Tate T2 (pp. 150) is the stable-subspace clause of finite-potent-trace-calculus, followed by isomorphism-of-pairs invariance. Step 5: Ω is generated by f dg (kahler-differentials presentation) and all three residues are k-linear. Edge cases checked: N=0, N=V, A a submodule, and k((t))² with res(t⁻¹dt)=2=1+1 including characteristic 2. No duplicate exact-sequence node was found. Batch-5 flag: lem-trf-vector-subspace-complement is a Mathlib-leaf linear-algebra fact (vector-space complements) depending only on def-weil-field. It is not a step of the trace formula or Poincaré duality proof, so it is accepted. No fixes.
